title: Assembly Language – Question Paper
instructions: Answer all questions. Use the 9618 assembly instruction set in the back of the paper. Calculators are not permitted.

questions.text: In the instruction `LDD 20`, what does **20** represent?

options.text: The absolute memory address 20 to load the value from
The value 20 is loaded directly into the accumulator (immediate addressing)

questions.explanation: LDD <value> uses immediate addressing — the operand is the data itself. LDM loads the contents of a memory address.

questions.text: Which instruction type is `STO 300`?

options.text: Direct addressing — stores ACC at the memory address 300

questions.explanation: STO always stores the contents of the accumulator into the stated address.

questions.text: State the difference between a **register**, a **general purpose register** and the **accumulator**.

answer.text: A register is a small, very fast storage location inside the CPU.

General purpose registers (GPRs) are used to hold data/addresses temporarily during processing, whereas the accumulator is a special register that automatically stores the result of arithmetic/logic operations.

questions.explanation: Special purpose registers have a fixed task; GPRs are for temporary general data — Cambridge uses registers numbered 0–7.

questions.text: What would be stored in the accumulator after executing `LDD 5` then `INC` then `INC`?
questions.explanation: LDD 5 puts 5 in the ACC; each INC adds 1, so 5 → 6 → 7.

questions.text: The instruction `STA 500` is executed on a 9618 machine. Explain what the mnemonic and the operand mean and what the operation does to the memory.

answer.text: STA = store accumulator; 500 is the absolute memory address.
The contents of the ACC are copied to memory location 500 (existing contents there are overwritten; the ACC keeps its value).

questions.explanation: STA is the same operation as STO in the 9618 instruction set.

questions.text: Explain how the **fetch–decode–execute (FDE)** cycle uses the **registers PC, MAR, MDR, CIR and the control unit** during the **fetch** stage.

answer.text: PC holds the address of the next instruction; the address is copied to the MAR.
The instruction at that address is fetched from memory into the MDR (via the data bus).
The instruction is copied into the CIR and the PC is incremented.
The control unit decodes the instruction and issues the signals needed to carry it out (execute stage).

questions.explanation: Order matters: PC → MAR → memory → MDR → CIR, PC + 1, then CU decodes.

questions.text: Which of the following is **NOT** part of the Von Neumann architecture?
questions.explanation: Von Neumann components: CU, ALU, registers (incl. ACC), buses and the single shared memory for data and instructions.

questions.text: Describe **two** differences between the **address bus** and the **data bus**.

answer.text: The address bus is (normally) unidirectional — CPU to memory only; the data bus is bidirectional.
The width of the address bus determines the number of addressable memory locations; the width of the data bus determines how many bits can be transferred at once.
Any further correct difference, e.g. address bus carries where data goes, data bus carries the instruction/data itself.

questions.explanation: If the address bus is n bits then 2ⁿ locations can be addressed.

questions.text: Assembly language cannot be executed directly by a CPU. Explain why, naming the translator used.

answer.text: The CPU can only execute machine code (binary opcodes); assembly uses mnemonics.
An assembler translates each assembly instruction into its machine-code equivalent (often one instruction to one opcode).

questions.explanation: Assembly is a low-level language with a direct 1:1 relationship to machine code, translated by an assembler.

questions.text: Which register holds the instruction currently being decoded/executed?
questions.explanation: CIR (current instruction register) holds the instruction under decode. IC is the register-transfer notation synonym in 9618.

questions.text:
The program below is run. State the contents of memory address 300 and of the accumulator immediately after the last instruction.

```
LDD 12
ADD 8
STO 300
LDD 4
STA 300
```

answer.text: LDD 12 then ADD 8 → ACC = 20
STO 300 → memory[300] = 20
LDD 4 then STA 300 overwrites → memory[300] = 4 and ACC = 4

questions.explanation: Final: ACC = 4; memory[300] = 4. Watch for the overwrite — a classic trap.

questions.text:
Trace the program and complete the table for the accumulator after each instruction.

```
LDD 6
MUL 3
SUB 4
DIV 2
```

(Use integer division.)
Write assembly language code to calculate **Y = (A + B) × 2**, where A and B are already stored in memory addresses 200 and 201. Store the result in address 202.

answer.text: LDM 200 (loads A into the ACC)
ADD 201 / LDM 201 then ADD — A + B in ACC
SHL 1 (shift left 1 = multiply by 2), or LDD 2 then MUL
STO 202 to store the result

questions.explanation:
LDM 200
ADD 201
SHL 1
STO 202

Note: ADD 201 will not work if 201 is meant as a value — use LDM 201 into a second register or store/load via memory.

questions.text: What does the instruction `SHL 1` do to the contents of the accumulator?

options.text: Multiplies it by 2 (shift left one place)

questions.explanation: Logical shift left by 1 place doubles the value; each place shifted left doubles, right halves.

questions.text: Explain what is meant by **bit manipulation** and give **two** examples of its practical use.

answer.text: Performing operations directly on individual bits of a binary value, using AND/OR/XOR/NOT and shifts (masking, setting, clearing, toggling).
Example 1 — masking with AND to check/test/clear specific bits (e.g. colour channels, flags).
Example 2 — shift left/right for fast multiply/divide by powers of 2, or to pack several flags into one byte.

questions.explanation: Bit manipulation is also used for encryption, compression and low-level device control registers.

questions.text: An **interrupt** occurs during program execution. Describe the two possible **classes of interrupt** (in terms of where they come from).

answer.text: Hardware interrupt — generated by a hardware device (e.g. keyboard press, printer out of paper, disk ready).
Software interrupt — generated by the running program (e.g. division by zero, an error, or a scheduled service).

questions.explanation: After the ISR finishes, the previous program state is restored from the stack and execution continues.

questions.text: Why does the CPU save the contents of its registers to the **stack** when an interrupt occurs?

options.text: To make the processor run faster
So the current state can be restored and the interrupted program can continue correctly
To permanently store the program on disk
To clear the RAM for the ISR

questions.explanation: The stack stores the return address and register values; the ISR runs, then pops them back (LIFO).

questions.text: Explain the difference between **direct**, **indirect** and **indexed** addressing, giving one instruction from the 9618 set for each.

answer.text: Direct: the operand is the memory address holding the data — e.g. LDM 300 / STO 300.
Indirect: the operand is the address of an address (a pointer) — e.g. LDI 300 — the CPU reads 300 to find the real address.
Indexed: the effective address is the operand plus the contents of the index register, used to access array elements — e.g. LDX 300.
Immediate addressing named as the fourth type — the operand IS the value (LDD 20).

questions.explanation: Use LDM/LDD/LDI/LDX/STX correctly — the exam papers do not forgive a wrong mnemonic.

questions.text: Which statement about **RISC** compared with **CISC** is correct?

options.text: RISC has fewer, simpler instructions that each take one clock cycle

questions.explanation: RISC = reduced instruction set: few simple instructions, fixed length, one cycle each, more registers, heavy pipelining. CISC = many specialised instructions, variable length.

questions.text: The 9618 instruction set uses register-transfer notation. Write the register-transfer notation for `LDD 5` followed by `ADD 3`.

answer.text: LDD 5 → ACC ← 5 (or IX ← 5 where IX is the accumulator/index register)
ADD 3 → ACC ← ACC + 3

questions.explanation: Cambridge 9618 writes the accumulator as IX. Register-transfer notation shows data movement with arrows, e.g. ACC ← ACC + 3.
